title: Witness
hookLine: survivors rebuilt lives and told what happened
carry: the listening is the next link

lines: A STORY NOBODY WANTED TO HEAR.
cards: What do you do with something you saw that the world would rather not hear? Some survivors said that after the war, the people around them changed the subject. So they did the next thing.
They married. They worked. They raised children, learned new languages, opened shops in cities they'd never heard of as children.
And some of them, sometimes many years later, sat down in front of a microphone, or a classroom, or a camera, and began to say what happened. Slowly. With names.
Today's word is what they became.

teach.h: ED: ONE WHO SAW, AND TELLS.
teach.b: In Hebrew, a witness is an ed. The Torah takes witnesses seriously. Leviticus says that someone who has seen or known a thing, and is called to testify, and stays silent, carries the guilt.
To have seen is to owe something.
And the prophet Isaiah turns a whole people into witnesses: "Ye are My witnesses, saith the LORD." In Hebrew, atem edai. The survivors took up that word in their own way.
They wrote memoirs and kept the diaries they'd hidden.
At the trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, survivors took the stand one after another and told the court what they'd lived through.
They sat for recorded interviews, now kept in archives like those at Yad Vashem, the USC Shoah Foundation and Yale's Fortunoff archive. Being a witness cost something; every telling meant going back.
Some survivors could never speak of it at all, and their silence is part of the record too.
Elie Wiesel, a survivor and writer, put the next step this way: whoever listens to a witness becomes a witness. The survivors will not always be here to speak.
But their words are, and whoever hears them carries something forward.

how: Jewish schools, museums and communities invite survivors into classrooms and memorial gatherings, and play recorded testimonies there too, especially around Yom HaShoah.

games.q: you survived. many years later, a student asks you what happened. what do you do?
o: send the student to a book.
games.why: survivors who told became witnesses, and whoever listened, Elie Wiesel said, became one too. the history also honors those who couldn't speak.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen to the sounds around you: the room, the street, your own breath.

Listen the way you'd listen to someone telling you something that matters, not to fix it or answer it, only to receive it. If you pray, ask for an open ear; if not, simply practice the listening itself.

wordCard.voice: Witness. In Hebrew, ed: someone who saw, and tells. Survivors who told what happened became witnesses for everyone who came after.
